title: The option for the poor
hook: a rich man passes a poor man at his gate every day, and never once sees him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cain's dodge, and the answer: yes. Your line was rights and duties. When you named what you were owed, did you name what you owe? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-six.

A rich man's gate. He goes in and out in purple and fine linen, and feasts every day. At the same gate lies a poor man covered in sores, wishing for the crumbs that fall from the table. Jesus tells this story in Luke, and two details stand out. The poor man has a name, Lazarus; the rich man never gets one. And the rich man is never cruel. He doesn't kick Lazarus or send him away. He simply does nothing for him, day after day. Catholic social teaching has a phrase meant to make that kind of passing by hard. Today, the preferential option for the poor.
screen: `A RICH MAN'S GATE.` → `THE POOR MAN HAS A NAME.` → `THE RICH MAN DOES NOTHING.`

segments.voice: First, what preferential means here. It doesn't mean God loves poor people more and everyone else less. At a family table, if one child is sick, that child gets served first, and nobody thinks the others are loved less. The Catechism speaks of the Church's preferential love for those oppressed by poverty in that sense: the ones in greatest need get attention first. Second, where it comes from. In Luke, Jesus opens his teaching on the plain like this, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are ye poor, for yours is the kingdom of God." The Greek word there is ptochos, a word for the poor who depend on others to live. Not a footnote to the gospel; the first blessing in that sermon. Third, what it isn't. It isn't meant to set one class against another, and it isn't a task for the poor alone. It is asked of every Christian, rich and poor alike. John Paul the Second called it a special form of primacy in the exercise of Christian charity. Fourth, how it works. The phrase gives a lens for judging any decision, from a nation's budget to a parish schedule to a household's spending: how does this land on the people with the least? Who is lying at this particular gate? Back in the story, the rich man's failure wasn't one cruel choice against Lazarus. It was ordinary choices, day after day, made as if Lazarus weren't there.
screen: `SERVED FIRST, NOT LOVED MORE.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE YE POOR.` · `NOT AGAINST ANYONE.` · then: `A LENS FOR EVERY DECISION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at one decision from a poor person's view. Settle, and breathe. Pick a decision in front of you this week. Where to shop. How to vote on something. A rule at work. What to do with an extra bit of money. Now walk around to the other side of the gate. Who in your town has the least, and how does this decision land on them? You don't need to change your mind. Just let yourself see from there for a moment. If you pray, you can hold that person before God. The bell holds the time.
Preferential option for the poor. In Catholic teaching, the needs of the poor come first in judging any decision, the way a sick child is served first. Today's word.
screen: `PREFERENTIAL OPTION FOR THE POOR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the poor first. Today, before one decision, ask who's lying at the gate, and give them the first look. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Catholics live this through parish food pantries, the Society of St. Vincent de Paul, Catholic Charities and similar works, and through advocacy that asks how laws and budgets affect the poor.

fork.setup: you're the poor man lying at the rich man's gate, hungry and covered in sores. what does the story say you long for?
options: the crumbs that fall from the table.
fork.reveal: Lazarus wishes only for the crumbs from the rich man's table. the story's sting is how little he asks, and that no one gives it to him.

original.note: Greek: poor, one who depends on others to live. Luke's word in "blessed are ye poor."

notes: Ptochos glossed as 'the poor who depend on others to live' (standard lexicon sense: dependent, beggarly). Confirm.
'The first blessing in that sermon': Luke 6:20 is the first of the Beatitudes in Luke's sermon on the plain; confirm wording.
The sick-child image is an analogy, not a Church text; confirm it fairly represents 'preferential' in CCC 2448 and SRS 42.
'It isn't a class war' paraphrases the Church's insistence that the option is not exclusive or partisan; a Keeper may want a specific citation.
The index title stays 'The option for the poor'; the history of the phrase (Latin American bishops) is left out under the claims rule.

Editor: the rich man no longer 'never sees' Lazarus (in Luke 16:24 he knows him by name); now he 'does nothing for him', in hook, screen, myth and fork. Cut the stock 'easy to miss'; softened the unsourced 'the Church says it isn't a class war'.
